title: A review of chemical ‘spot’ tests: A presumptive illicit drug identification technique

claims.statement: In one laboratory study of a three-reagent colour kit for ecstasy (Marquis, Mecke and Simon's reagents; a DanceSafe kit bought online, without lot numbers), compared with GC-MS or the known identity of the drugs, readings by experienced analysts matched whether MDMA was present, readings by two testers new to the kit did not, and a positive reading never showed a second drug. Three experienced analysts using the kit's instructions and colour charts read all 35 seized samples that contained MDMA as positive and the four without MDMA as negative, except that one analyst read one of the four, which held no identifiable drug, as weakly positive (editors' Wilson 95% CI 90.1–100% for 35 of 35, 51.0–100% for 4 of 4); the seven MDMA samples that also held caffeine, ephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA read like the rest. Two testers trained in pharmacology but new to the kit, given eight samples of known drugs and only the kit's leaflet, diverged: one read both MDMA samples as negative, the other read codeine, dihydrocodeine, dextromethorphan and morphine as MDMA or MDMA-like; together 2 of 4 MDMA readings were positive and 7 of 12 non-MDMA readings negative, and with the Marquis reagent alone 10 of the 12 non-MDMA readings were positive (Murray et al., 2003). A laboratory comparison from an unpublished thesis, known only from a narrative review (156 amnesty-bin samples, Marquis read by laboratory staff before GC-MS), found the MDMA colour (purple, blue or black) in all 53 samples with MDMA-like substances and in no others, while the amphetamine colour appeared in 21 samples without amphetamine; its table holds 187 entries for 156 samples (Winstock et al., 2001). Two narrative reviews add, second-hand, that colour tests are presumptive: MDMA, MDEA and MDA give similar colours, other substances react too (the Marquis reagent also with aspirin and sugar), more than one drug or tablet dyes can change the result, and the tests show no amount (Winstock et al., 2001; Philp & Fu, 2018). No sample contained PMA, MDA or methamphetamine on its own, and the kit and drug market were those of the early 2000s. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Murray et al. Part I (experienced analysts, three reagents): 35/35 MDMA samples positive (Wilson 90.1–100%, editors' calculation); 4/4 non-MDMA negative for two analysts (51.0–100%), 3/4 for the third (one weak positive); 7 samples with a second drug read like MDMA alone. Part II (two novices, 8 known drugs, three reagents): sensitivity 2/4 (50%), specificity 7/12 (58%), positive and negative predictive values 2/7 and 7/9 (printed 28% and 77%); Novice A 0/2 MDMA detected and 5/6 others negative, Novice B 2/2 and 2/6; Marquis alone 10 false positives in 12 non-MDMA readings and 2 false negatives. Winstock et al. (second-hand, Murphy 1999): purple/blue/black 53/53 MDMA-like and 0 others; orange/brown 47 amphetamine samples and 21 without; 187 cell entries for n = 156.
